description: We are a team of 3 (AI Lead, Full-Stack Dev, UI/3D/Video Designer) building an AI research platform on NASA microgravity fire data (BASS-II, SAFFIRE). Since web and design are set, we want 1 or 2 strong teammates: (1) AI/Data/Python specialist to parse raw NASA datasets and build pipelines, (2) Researcher/Writer to verify experiment details and write our study. Send a request to join!
summary:
In zero gravity, hot air does not rise and fire behaves completely differently than on Earth, turning into slow, nearly invisible blue spheres that release toxic gases in confined spacecraft cabins. As future Artemis, Lunar Gateway, and Mars missions shift toward lower pressure and higher oxygen environments, engineers need reliable spaceflight evidence before selecting cabin materials. Over two decades, NASA conducted dozens of orbital fire experiments, yet the findings remain scattered across tens of thousands of disconnected files and technical reports.

LAMINAR is a microgravity combustion research observatory that turns NASA Physical Sciences Informatics data into an interactive, traceable safety tool. Our platform unifies all 26 official NASA combustion investigations, 2281 cross mission experimental runs, and 129 calibrated International Space Station burns into a clean exploration workflow. Engineers and researchers can inspect parametric 3D flight chambers, plot gas changes across airflow regimes, and ask safety questions through a verified evidence desk that links every claim directly to original NASA report pages and spreadsheet rows while blocking invalid cross material comparisons.
details:
What LAMINAR Does and How It Works

LAMINAR is an interactive scientific observatory built for spacecraft fire safety engineers, mission planners, and combustion researchers. Instead of forcing users to download and manually cross check thousands of raw repository files, the platform guides users through five connected stages covering discovery, mission exploration, 3D chamber inspection, evidence analysis, and source verification.

We cataloged all 26 official NASA Physical Sciences Informatics combustion search results and mapped 66998 repository file nodes totaling 12.77 tebibytes. Because over 99 percent of that archive consists of raw high speed camera video that remains linked directly on NASA servers, we built a reproducible ingestion pipeline that downloaded, checksummed with SHA 256, and indexed 455 compact reports, spreadsheets, and official NASA historical and spinoff documents into 14227 searchable text passages and 2281 structured experimental runs. For the 129 calibrated Burning and Suppression of Solids II flight burns on the International Space Station, we normalized gas concentration measurements and sensor uncertainty bounds across seven distinct material and geometry cohorts.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Earth based flammability tests cannot predict how plastics, fabrics, and wires burn without buoyancy, especially in upcoming lunar and deep space habitats operating at 34 percent oxygen and 56.5 kilopascals. LAMINAR compresses days of manual literature and spreadsheet review into seconds of audit ready evidence. Beyond space exploration, the platform connects orbital smoke aerosol and flame suppression findings to life saving firefighter breathing tanks, low false alarm smoke detectors, and protective gear on Earth.

Creativity and Scientific Safeguards

Rather than building a generic chatbot or averaging incompatible experiments into misleading safety scores, we created a hybrid neuro symbolic evidence desk. Deterministic Python solvers calculate gas partial pressures, multi component mixture viscosity, and Reynolds numbers while enforcing strict scientific guardrails that refuse invalid cross cohort comparisons and flag small sample sizes. When Gemini synthesizes a plain language explanation, an automated verification firewall checks every number and citation against retrieved NASA records and falls back to deterministic extraction if any claim lacks direct support. Users can also inspect parametric 3D hardware models built from published NASA duct dimensions across six apparatus modes, alongside an interactive variable coverage matrix showing what NASA has and has not measured.

Tools, Languages, and Technologies Used

We built the backend using Python, FastAPI, SQLite in read only mode, Pydantic validation schemas, and custom BM25 retrieval and thermodynamic calculation modules. The frontend uses TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, custom SVG charts, and Three.js with WebGL2 rendering for interactive 3D apparatus inspection. We also integrated the Gemini API as an optional citation locked synthesis layer.
